exact_wording: 3.—(1) This section applies as between contracting parties where one of them deals as consumer or on the other's written standard terms of business. summary: Where one party deals as consumer or contracts on the other's written standard terms, clauses letting the other party exclude liability for its own breach, or perform substantially differently or not at all, must satisfy the s.11 reasonableness test.

exact_wording: 11.—(1) In relation to a contract term, the requirement of reasonableness for the purposes of this Part and section 3 of the Misrepresentation Act 1967 is that the term shall have been a fair and reasonable one to be included having regard to the circumstances which were, or ought reasonably to have been, known to or in the contemplation of the parties when the contract was made. (2) In determining for the purposes of section 6 or 7 whether a contract term satisfies the requirement of reasonableness, regard shall be had in particular to the matters specified in the Second Schedule; but this subsection does not prevent the court or arbitrator from holding, in accordance with any rule of law, that a term which purports to exclude or restrict any relevant liability is not a term of the contract. (4) Where by reference to a contract term or notice a person seeks to restrict liability to a specified sum of money, and the question arises (under this or any other Act) whether the term or notice satisfies the requirement of reasonableness, regard shall be had in particular (but without prejudice to subsection (2) in the case of contract terms) to (a) the resources which he could expect to be available to him for the purpose of meeting the liability should it arise; and (b) how far it was open to him to cover himself by insurance. (5) It is for those claiming that a contract term or notice satisfies the requirement of reasonableness to show that it does.
summary: Defines the statutory reasonableness test used throughout UCTA and imported into s.3 of the Misrepresentation Act 1967: fairness judged at contract formation, with the Second Schedule guidelines applying to ss.6/7, specific resources/insurance factors for monetary liability caps, and the burden of proof on the party relying on the term.
applicability_conditions: a UCTA s.2(2), s.3, s.6(3), s.7(3), or Misrepresentation Act s.3 trigger has independently fired and reasonableness must now be assessed

exact_wording: 12.—(1) A party to a contract “deals as consumer” in relation to another party if (a) he neither makes the contract in the course of a business nor holds himself out as doing so; (b) the other party does make the contract in the course of a business; and (c) in the case of a contract governed by the law of sale of goods or hire-purchase, or by section 7, the goods passing under or in pursuance of the contract are of a type ordinarily supplied for private use or consumption. (2) But on a sale by auction or by competitive tender the buyer is not in any circumstances to be regarded as dealing as consumer. (3) Subject to this, it is for those claiming that a party does not deal as consumer to show that he does not.
summary: Defines 'dealing as consumer': the counterparty must not be contracting in the course of a business (or holding itself out as doing so), the other party must be, and (for goods contracts) the goods must be of a type ordinarily supplied for private use. Auction/competitive-tender buyers are never consumers, and the burden is on whoever asserts non-consumer status.
applicability_conditions: needed as an input predicate whenever a UCTA module's applicability depends on whether a party 'deals as consumer' (e.g. ss.3, 6, 7)
trigger_keywords: in the course of a business

exact_wording: The matters to which regard is to be had in particular for the purposes of sections 6(3) and 7(3) and (4) are any of the following which appear to be relevant: (a) the strength of the bargaining positions of the parties relative to each other, taking into account (among other things) alternative means by which the customer's requirements could have been met; (b) whether the customer received an inducement to agree to the term, or in accepting it had an opportunity of entering into a similar contract with other persons, but without having to accept a similar term; (c) whether the customer knew or ought reasonably to have known of the existence and extent of the term (having regard, among other things, to any custom of the trade and any previous course of dealing between the parties); (d) where the term excludes or restricts any relevant liability if some condition is not complied with, whether it was reasonable at the time of the contract to expect that compliance with that condition would be practicable; (e) whether the goods were manufactured, processed or adapted to the special order of the customer.
summary: The specific reasonableness guidelines for ss.6(3)/7(3)-(4): relative bargaining strength, inducements/alternative sources, the customer's knowledge of the term, practicability of any compliance condition, and whether goods were custom-made.
applicability_conditions: a s.6(3) or s.7(3)/(4) exclusion clause is being assessed for reasonableness

exact_wording: 26.—(1) The limits imposed by this Act on the extent to which a person may exclude or restrict liability by reference to a contract term do not apply to liability arising under such a contract as is described in subsection (3). (2) The terms of such a contract are not subject to any requirement of reasonableness under section 3 or 4. (3) Subject to subsection (4), that description of contract is one whose characteristics are the following: (a) either it is a contract of sale of goods or it is one under or in pursuance of which the possession or ownership of goods passes; and (b) it is made by parties whose places of business (or, if they have none, habitual residences) are in the territories of different States.
summary: UCTA's limits (including the reasonableness requirement) do not apply at all to qualifying international supply contracts — sale-of-goods or goods-passing contracts between parties based in different States, meeting the cross-border delivery/formation conditions in s.26(4). This is a full carve-out, not a reasonableness factor, and should be checked before any UCTA trigger fires.
applicability_conditions: the contract is a sale of goods, or one under which possession/ownership of goods passes
the contracting parties' places of business (or habitual residences) are in different States
the contract meets at least one of the s.26(4) cross-border conditions (goods in international carriage, offer/acceptance in different States, or delivery specified to a different State)

engine_revision_notes: v2 revision: added 'ip_agreement' to applicable_contract_types. Sample contract review (Armstrong Flooring / AFI Licensing Intellectual Property Agreement) showed this contract type has no home in the original taxonomy (sale_of_goods/services/lease/nda/distribution/employment/other_unclassified) despite containing CRTPA-relevant indemnification and third-party-beneficiary language. The substantive ss.2-4 chunks (s2_1, s2_2, s3, s6_1, s6_2_3, s7_3a, s7_2_3) deliberately do NOT get ip_agreement added to their own applicable_contract_types, since they should never be eligible to fire on this contract type in the first place.
